column2: The UK NCSC reports that actors exploited routers and modified DHCP DNS settings to redirect traffic through attacker-controlled DNS servers and facilitate adversary-in-the-middle attacks.
column8: Consistent technical reporting from NCSC and Black Lotus Labs; Lumen describes its own network telemetry, although investigative dependencies require further assessment.
column13: Router-based DNS manipulation and traffic redirection are supported by overlapping technical reporting; the full campaign scope and attribution remain separately assessed.
column15: Underlying forensic evidence is not fully public; campaign activity extends from 2024 into 2026; independence of individual findings requires further assessment.
column18: Source section: Executive summary and APT28 malicious DNS activity. Grade 2 means probably true; technical corroboration does not establish attribution.

column2: The UK NCSC assesses that APT28 is almost certainly Russian GRU Unit 26165 and attributes the router exploitation and DNS hijacking activity to APT28.
column8: Official attribution is documented; supporting independent attribution evidence has not yet been evaluated.
column13: Record as NCSC attribution rather than independently established responsibility.
column15: Public advisory does not provide the complete underlying attribution evidence.
column18: Source section: Introduction. Grade 6 is provisional and means not yet judged.

column2: CERT Polska reports that destructive activity on 29 December 2025 damaged remote terminal units at Polish wind and photovoltaic grid connection points, disrupting communications with distribution system operator systems and preventing remote control, while electricity production continued.
column8: CERT Polska reports direct incident investigation and describes the affected devices and operational consequences; underlying forensic artefacts have not been independently reproduced in this assessment.
column13: The reported impact was loss of remote communications and control, not interruption of electricity generation; the scale of device damage at individual installations remains to be established.
column15: Currently supported by one investigating organisation; individual site-level forensic evidence and independent impact confirmation have not been evaluated.
column18: Source: CERT Polska Energy Sector Incident Report, Attack on Renewable Energy Plants section; information credibility grade 2 is provisional and applies to this specific impact claim, not threat-actor attribution.

column2: CERT Polska reports that affected Polish renewable-energy facilities used internet-exposed FortiGate VPN interfaces permitting authentication without MFA; attackers obtained administrative access to these devices, but incomplete logs prevented confirmation of the original compromise mechanism.
column8: CERT Polska documents the exposed VPN configuration and attacker privileges through incident investigation; missing device logs prevent determination of the precise entry mechanism.
column13: The exposed VPN interfaces represent a potential access path, not proof that attackers exploited a particular vulnerability or initially obtained access through a specific credential compromise.
column15: Complete FortiGate logs were unavailable; prior vulnerability exposure and possible credential reuse are contextual findings rather than confirmed initial-access mechanisms.
column18: Source: CERT Polska technical PDF, Attack Vector on the GCP, page 7; distinguish observed administrative access from hypotheses about how it was obtained.

column2: CERT Polska reports that after gaining internal network access at Polish renewable-energy grid connection points, attackers conducted reconnaissance and executed a partially automated destructive plan involving controller firmware damage, system-file deletion and custom wiper malware; damage to RTUs resulted in loss of remote communications and control.
column8: CERT Polska describes the sequence of reconnaissance and destructive activity based on its incident investigation; the precise actions and affected device types at each installation have not been independently verified in this assessment.
column13: The reporting supports a destructive campaign against industrial and supporting systems; it does not establish that every listed destructive technique was used against every affected RTU.
column15: Public summary aggregates activity across multiple grid connection points; device-specific forensic artefacts and exact technique-to-device relationships require further validation.
column18: Source: CERT Polska Energy Sector Incident Report, Attack on Renewable Energy Plants section; do not infer confirmed default-credential use or assign MITRE ATT&CK techniques solely from this aggregated description.

column2: CERT Polska associates the coordinated 29 December 2025 cyberattacks in Poland with the activity cluster identified as Static Tundra, Berserk Bear, Ghost Blizzard and Dragonfly, citing substantial overlap in attack infrastructure and network activity.
column8: CERT Polska describes technical infrastructure overlap supporting its cluster association; the underlying comparison has not been independently reproduced in this project.
column13: The reported infrastructure overlap supports association with the named activity cluster but does not independently establish direction by a specific Russian state organisation.
column15: Attribution evidence has not been independently replicated; compromised infrastructure may be shared or reused; equivalence of vendor cluster labels and the Russian state organisational connection require separate evaluation.
column18: See analytical-notes/poland-energy-attribution-assessment.md; information credibility grade 2 applies to the reported cluster association, not independent proof of Russian intelligence-service responsibility.

column2: Cisco Talos assesses Static Tundra as a Russian state-sponsored cyberespionage actor associated with Energetic Bear and the Russian FSB's Center 16; this historical attribution does not independently establish responsibility for the December 2025 Polish attacks.
column8: Cisco Talos presents specialist threat intelligence research and references historical government findings; the underlying evidence connecting the activity cluster to a specific Russian state organisation has not been independently reproduced in this project.
column13: Cisco Talos provides historical Russian state-attribution context for Static Tundra; CERT Polska's separate infrastructure analysis remains the primary evidence associating the cluster with the Polish incidents.
column15: Historical actor attribution and vendor cluster equivalence require further examination; the publication predates the December 2025 attacks and cannot corroborate their incident-specific attribution.
column18: Source: Cisco Talos Static Tundra research; related analytical note: analytical-notes/poland-energy-attribution-assessment.md; no incident IDs assigned because this claim concerns historical actor attribution.

column2: CERT Polska reports that attackers accessed the operational technology network of a Polish combined heat-and-power facility through a private APN; investigators identified a network misconfiguration permitting arbitrary devices within the private APN to communicate with one another as a contributing factor.
column8: CERT Polska reports reconstructing the attack path from collected incident evidence and identifying a private APN configuration weakness; the underlying forensic evidence has not been independently reproduced in this project.
column13: The private APN configuration permitted communications between devices that should not necessarily have been able to reach one another; this supports an access-path finding but does not independently establish the attacker's original method of gaining access to the APN.
column15: The full sequence of attacker access and the role of any additional weaknesses require detailed examination of the technical report; no specific credential compromise or software vulnerability exploitation is established by this claim.
column18: Source: CERT Polska August 2026 follow-up report; related incident INC-005; private APN network reachability must be distinguished from the original compromise mechanism.

column2: CERT Polska reports that the December 2025 cyberattack against a second Polish combined heat-and-power facility resulted in the shutdown of a steam turbine and process-water treatment system, temporarily interrupting cogeneration while residential heat supplies remained uninterrupted.
column8: CERT Polska describes the operational consequences identified during its follow-up investigation; the reported distinction between interrupted cogeneration and continued residential heat delivery is specific to this facility.
column13: The attack reportedly disrupted energy-production processes without interrupting residential heat delivery; the precise duration and complete extent of operational consequences have not been independently established.
column15: Underlying industrial-system logs and operational records have not been independently examined; the available reporting does not establish every affected component or the full duration of disruption.
column18: Source: CERT Polska August 2026 follow-up report; related incident INC-005; distinguish shutdown of production equipment from interruption of consumer heat supply.

column2: The UK NCSC announced that the UK and EU member states formally attributed the December 2025 cyberattack against Poland's energy infrastructure to Russia's FSB Centre 16.
column8: Official UK government announcement describing a multinational attribution decision; the announcement establishes the reported government position but does not publicly disclose the complete underlying intelligence or forensic evidence.
column13: The announcement provides direct evidence of the stated UK and EU attribution position; it does not independently demonstrate the underlying technical attribution or establish the role of FSB Centre 16 in every individual incident recorded in the Polish dataset.
column15: Underlying intelligence is not fully publicly inspectable; participating states' evidentiary contributions and their independence from CERT Polska findings have not been established; incident-level applicability requires separate assessment.
column18: Source: UK NCSC July 2026 announcement; relevant to the December 2025 Polish energy operation; distinguish formal government attribution from independently verified forensic attribution.

column2: A July 2026 multinational cybersecurity advisory reports that FSB Centre 16 actors scan for network devices with exposed SNMP services and weak or default community strings, use SNMP requests to copy and transfer device configurations to attacker-controlled infrastructure, and sometimes exploit known Cisco vulnerabilities.
column8: The joint advisory describes specific network-device exploitation and collection procedures including SNMP Set-Requests, configuration-file transfers and exploitation of known Cisco vulnerabilities; the earlier FBI advisory reports related network-device exploitation and configuration collection, but overlapping evidence and underlying investigative data have not been independently verified.
column9: Partially overlapping reporting; independent corroboration not established
column12: Reported activity attributed to FSB Centre 16
column13: The described techniques provide a technically specific account of router-focused reconnaissance, configuration collection and exploitation; the advisory concerns worldwide activity and does not identify a sufficiently specific new European victim incident.
column15: The July 2026 multinational advisory references earlier FBI reporting; SRC-014 provides related original government-reported observations but must not be counted as independent corroboration of SRC-010. Overlap with Cisco Talos research and the independence of underlying observations remain unresolved; technical findings do not independently prove actor attribution or applicability to the December 2025 Polish incidents.
column18: Sources: SRC-010 technical details and Appendix A; SRC-014 FBI advisory dated 2025-08-20. The FBI advisory predates the multinational advisory and reports related network-device exploitation and configuration collection, without identifying a distinct European victim. TTP-003 maps the reported SNMP-triggered configuration-file collection to Enterprise ATT&CK T1602.002 (Network Device Configuration Dump); T1602.001 was considered but not assigned because a conventional MIB dump was not established; T1595.001, T1595.002 and T1190 remain candidate mappings requiring separate evidence assessment.

column2: During an April 15 2026 government press briefing Sweden's Minister for Civil Defence reported that an unnamed heating plant in western Sweden experienced an unsuccessful attempted destructive cyberattack in spring 2025; protective systems reportedly prevented serious consequences; the Swedish Security Service reportedly identified a pro-Russian actor with connections to Russian intelligence and security services.
column8: Direct government briefing statement supports that Swedish authorities publicly reported the incident and their attribution assessment; underlying technical investigation and Security Service findings have not been independently examined.
column9: Official government disclosure; independent forensic corroboration not established
column12: Swedish government-reported actor association with Russian intelligence and security services
column13: The statement provides geographically specific evidence of a reported attempted destructive attack against Swedish energy infrastructure; no confirmed operational interruption or independently verified actor attribution is established.
column15: Facility identity and exact incident date undisclosed; no technical indicators or intrusion mechanism published; protective outcome and actor association are based on government statements. Swedish auto-generated captions of the original government briefing have been reviewed, but audio-level transcription accuracy remains unverified. No independent technical corroboration of attribution has been established.
column16: Primary government statement reviewed; underlying evidence unavailable
column18: Source: SRC-011, including official government briefing recording dated 15 April 2026. Swedish captions examined at 06:11–06:41 and 22:52–23:07. The minister described connections to Russian intelligence and security services as an assessment; this does not establish operational direction by Russian authorities. Registered as INC-006; no ATT&CK technique assigned.

column2: CERT-UA reports identifying three additional malicious Office documents exploiting CVE-2026-21509 during late January 2026; their content, associated URLs and other characteristics indicated cyberattacks targeting organisations in EU countries.
column8: CERT-UA provides primary technical reporting identifying three additional malicious documents and explains that their content, URLs and other characteristics indicate EU organisational targeting; the underlying samples, recipient information and investigative telemetry have not been independently examined.
column9: Single-source primary technical reporting; independent corroboration not yet established
column12: CERT-UA attributes the broader activity to UAC-0001 (APT28); incident-specific attribution not independently verified
column13: The reporting supports an assessed attempt to target EU-country organisations using malicious Office documents; it does not establish delivery to named EU recipients, successful exploitation, compromise or exfiltration.
column15: The EU organisations are not named; precise recipient identities, delivery outcomes, successful execution and independent forensic corroboration are unavailable in the reviewed material. Overlap with Zscaler ThreatLabz reporting remains unresolved.
column16: Original CERT-UA advisory text reviewed by analyst; claim-level assessment preliminary
column18: Source: SRC-012, CERT-UA#19542, 1 February 2026; original Ukrainian-language advisory text supplied and reviewed. The three additional EU-targeting documents are distinct from the reported email distribution to more than 60 predominantly Ukrainian government addresses. No incident or ATT&CK mapping assigned at this stage.

column2: Zscaler ThreatLabz reports that Operation Neusploit used malicious Office RTF documents exploiting CVE-2026-21509, with analysed payload chains involving MiniDoor and PixyNetLoader, PNG-embedded shellcode, Covenant Grunt and Filen-based command-and-control communications.
column8: Zscaler provides detailed technical analysis of malicious documents, malware components, execution mechanisms and associated indicators; the underlying samples and victim telemetry have not been independently reproduced or examined by this project.
column9: Technical overlap with SRC-012 CERT-UA reporting on CVE-2026-21509, Covenant and Filen; shared artefacts identified, but evidentiary independence remains unresolved.
column12: Zscaler attributes Operation Neusploit to APT28 with high confidence; this is the publisher assessment, not an independently confirmed project attribution.
column13: The source supports the reported existence and technical characteristics of malicious-document exploitation and associated malware capabilities; it does not establish successful compromise or exfiltration from a named European organisation.
column15: Independent malware execution or reverse-engineering has not been performed by this project. The provenance of shared samples, relationship between payload variants and specific European recipients, and actual victim outcomes remain unresolved.
column16: Original Zscaler publication reviewed by analyst; claim-level assessment preliminary
column18: Source: SRC-013, Zscaler ThreatLabz, Operation Neusploit, 2 February 2026. Related source SRC-012 provides overlapping technical reporting but is not yet treated as independent corroboration. Reported capabilities are distinguished from demonstrated victim impact. No incident or ATT&CK mapping assigned at this stage.

column2: Zscaler ThreatLabz reports that Operation Neusploit targeted users in Slovakia and Romania during January 2026, supported by Romanian- and Slovak-language social-engineering lures and geographically restricted payload delivery infrastructure.
column8: Zscaler provides primary technical reporting identifying Slovakia and Romania as targeted countries and describing localised lures and geographic restrictions on payload delivery; recipient-level telemetry has not been independently examined.
column9: Single-source country-specific targeting assessment; SRC-012 reports related EU targeting but independence and sample-level correspondence are unresolved.
column12: Zscaler attributes Operation Neusploit to APT28 with high confidence; this is the publisher assessment and not independently confirmed Russian state direction.
column13: The reported localisation and infrastructure restrictions support an assessment of deliberate attempted targeting of users in Slovakia and Romania; they do not establish delivery to named organisations or successful compromise.
column15: The original reporting does not publicly establish specific recipient organisations, confirmed execution on European victim systems, successful exfiltration or independent victim-level corroboration. Country-specific sectoral targeting remains unresolved.
column16: Original Zscaler publication reviewed by analyst; claim-level assessment preliminary
column18: Source: SRC-013, Zscaler ThreatLabz, Operation Neusploit, 2 February 2026. Related claims: CLM-013 CERT-UA EU targeting and CLM-014 Zscaler technical findings. SRC-012 is not counted as independent corroboration. Geographic targeting is distinguished from confirmed organisational compromise. No incident or ATT&CK mapping assigned.

column2: La Poste Groupe reports that distributed denial-of-service activity beginning on 22 December 2025 disrupted access to online postal and banking services, with renewed disruption reported on 1 January 2026. La Banque Postale subsequently reported that DDoS activity continued until 5 January 2026, while core banking systems remained operational.
column8: First-party operational reporting by the affected corporate group supports the described disruption; the retrospective bank account provides additional operational detail but does not constitute independent corroboration.
column9: Related operator reporting; independent corroboration not established
column13: The sources support disruption of online access and reported continuity of core banking systems; they do not establish compromise of banking infrastructure, customer-data theft, or Russian state involvement.
column15: Both sources originate within the La Poste corporate group; underlying traffic telemetry and independent forensic findings are unavailable. The precise relationship between the 1 January renewed wave and the 5 January endpoint is not independently verified.
column18: SRC-015 contains dated operator updates through 1 January 2026; SRC-016 is a 22 January 2026 retrospective. The bank separately reports peaks above 366 Gbps and 2.5 billion packets per second, but those measurements are not included in this operational-impact claim. Incident ID intentionally left blank pending scope and attribution assessment.

column2: La Tribune reported on 24 December 2025 that NoName057(16) had claimed on Telegram to disrupt La Poste's digital-identity service. The publication cited the service's reported continued accessibility and assessments from Baptiste Robert and Pierre Delcher questioning the claimed target and the absence of identified La Poste targets in observed NoName057(16) target-distribution activity.
column8: The source is a dated, attributable journalistic account containing named expert interviews and a description of a purported Telegram responsibility claim. Grade 2 applies only to the existence of the reported claim and documented expert challenges, not to the truth of operational responsibility. The original Telegram message and underlying technical observations have not been independently authenticated.
column9: Single publication combining original expert interviews with derivative operator and purported actor reporting; independent corroboration of operational attribution not established
column12: Disputed responsibility claim; operational responsibility unverified
column13: The reported claim does not establish that NoName057(16) conducted the wider La Poste DDoS operation. The claimed digital-identity target reportedly remained accessible during observation, and an expert reported no identified La Poste targets in observed group target-distribution activity. These discrepancies weaken attribution but do not conclusively exclude participation because DDoS effects can be intermittent and monitoring coverage is unknown. Russian state direction is not established.
column15: The original Telegram post and account provenance have not been authenticated; screenshot context and timing are incompletely verified; underlying target-distribution records, monitoring coverage and incident-specific traffic telemetry are unavailable. Named expert assessments do not independently establish the perpetrator.
column18: Related claim: CLM-016 records La Poste operational disruption without perpetrator attribution. SRC-017 is the sole registered source for this claim. Moderate confidence concerns accurate reporting of the disputed claim and expert challenges; confidence in NoName057(16) operational responsibility remains Low. No incident ID or ATT&CK mapping assigned.

column2: ESET Research reports detecting and blocking three DynoWiper samples deployed against a Polish energy organisation on 29 December 2025 and attributes the destructive activity to Sandworm with medium confidence, citing malware and operational similarities to previously investigated activity.
column8: ESET presents direct endpoint detection and malware-analysis findings supporting the reported destructive activity. Grade 2 applies to the documented observations and existence of ESET attribution, not independent proof that Sandworm was responsible.
column9: Original technical reporting from ESET; incident-level overlap and investigative independence relative to CERT Polska SRC-006 remain unresolved
column12: ESET-reported Sandworm attribution; organisational responsibility not independently established
column13: ESET provides technical evidence of attempted destructive malware execution and assesses Sandworm involvement with medium confidence. CERT Polska separately associates the wider December 2025 Polish attacks with Static Tundra based on infrastructure and network activity. The assessments may concern overlapping or different operational stages; available evidence does not establish whether one actor or multiple actors participated. The relationship to INC-003 is plausible but not confirmed.
column15: ESET did not observe initial access; complete victim telemetry and sample provenance are unavailable; malware similarities are not uniquely identifying; exact victim correspondence with INC-003 and the scope of shared evidence with CERT Polska remain unresolved.
column18: Related claims CLM-006 and CLM-010. Moderate analytical confidence applies to the accurate characterisation of ESET findings and the documented attribution discrepancy, not to Sandworm responsibility. Confidence in independently resolving the responsible state organisation remains Low. No incident ID or ATT&CK mapping assigned pending incident-specific corroboration.

column2: Dragos assesses with moderate confidence that ELECTRUM was responsible for the 29 December 2025 cyberattacks affecting Polish distributed energy infrastructure, reporting incident-response involvement and identifying destructive activity against systems supporting renewable electricity generation.
column8: Dragos is an established industrial cybersecurity research and incident-response organisation reporting direct involvement in the investigation. Information credibility grade 2 applies to the existence and accurate characterisation of its published assessment and reported observations, not independent proof of ELECTRUM responsibility.
column9: Dragos reports direct incident-response involvement but also references CERT Polska findings; the independence of the underlying attribution evidence is not established. ESET SRC-018 reports a related Sandworm attribution, but equivalence of actor classifications and victim-level overlap remain unresolved.
column12: Dragos-reported ELECTRUM attribution; organisational responsibility not independently established
column13: Dragos attributes the Polish distributed-energy attacks to ELECTRUM with moderate confidence. Its reported incident-response involvement provides a potentially distinct investigative perspective, but the public article does not disclose enough attribution evidence for independent reproduction. Historical overlap between ELECTRUM and Sandworm does not establish identical operators in this incident. CERT Polska separately associates the coordinated Polish attacks with Static Tundra. The attribution assessments should remain distinct pending incident-specific reconciliation.
column15: Detailed Dragos intelligence brief not confirmed as reviewed; complete forensic artefacts, victim-level mapping, attribution indicators and independence from CERT Polska investigative evidence are unavailable. INC-002 is a grouped incident and the relationship does not establish ELECTRUM involvement at every affected installation.
column18: Related claims CLM-006 and CLM-018. Moderate analytical confidence concerns the accurate characterisation of Dragos reporting and its relevance to INC-002, not independently verified ELECTRUM responsibility. Confidence in identifying the responsible state organisation remains Low. No additional incident IDs or ATT&CK mappings assigned.
